name: Vapi
description: Vapi is the plumbing behind AI phone agents: you wire a speech-to-text engine, an LLM, a voice and a phone number into one bot that answers or places calls. The $0.05/min headline is only Vapi's orchestration cut - most real setups land near $0.15/min all-in once the four providers are stacked. Builders use it to sell AI receptionists to local businesses at $500-2,000 a month, but it is a developer tool and the dashboard is not friendly.
pricing_details: Vapi charges $0.05 per minute as a platform (orchestration) fee, billed to the second, and passes through four provider costs at cost with no markup: speech-to-text (about $0.005-0.008/min, e.g. Deepgram Nova-3 streaming at $0.0077/min), the LLM (token-based and the single biggest variable - Vapi's own docs call it the largest cost you control, driven by system-prompt length and roughly five model calls per conversation turn), text-to-speech (about $0.05-0.36/min depending on the voice; ElevenLabs Business at $990/mo is what unlocks the cheap end), and telephony (about $0.0085-0.014/min on Twilio plus about $2/mo per number). There is no required monthly subscription on the self-serve Build plan - you pay usage only. Real all-in cost lands around $0.10-0.30 per minute once everything is stacked, and roughly $0.12-0.24/min on a mid-tier voice before LLM tokens. Worked examples: 500 minutes/month is about $75-125 all-in; 2,000 minutes about $300-500; 10,000 minutes about $1,500-2,500. Extras that surprise people: HIPAA compliance is a $2,000/mo add-on, Zero Data Retention is $1,000/mo, concurrent lines beyond the included 10 cost $10/line/month, and SMS or chat messages are $0.005 each. Build keeps call recordings for only 14 days (chat logs 30 days) and has no SSO, RBAC or SOC 2. The Scale plan is an annual contract with custom volume pricing that is quote-only - you cannot budget it from a spreadsheet. New accounts get trial credit (widely reported around $10, plus 60+ included usage minutes) with no credit card. Competitor snapshot: Retell AI about $0.07/min voice layer ($0.07-0.31 all-in), Bland AI $0.14/min flat on Start, Synthflow from about $0.08-0.09/min.
pros: The lowest published platform fee in the category - $0.05/min versus Bland's $0.14 flat rate - and every component is swappable, so a tuned budget stack (fast STT, small model, standard voice) can run closer to $0.12/min than the $0.24 a premium ElevenLabs voice pushes it to

The monetization math is the whole reason to learn it: a 500-minute/month receptionist costs roughly $75-125 in usage, and small businesses pay $500-2,000/month for one, so four or five clients cover every platform bill you will ever have and the rest is margin
Bring-your-own API keys get billed at $0 by Vapi, you get 10 concurrent calls included plus a real API and SDKs, and the free trial credit lets you test latency and quality before spending a cent
cons: The $0.05 is a headline, not a bill. Four separate vendors - STT, LLM, TTS and telephony - each add cost on top, so real spend lands around $0.10-0.30/min and you end up reconciling four invoices that all move independently when any provider changes rates

It is a builder's tool, not a turnkey product. There is no clean 'describe an agent, get a phone number' flow you can hand to a non-technical client, latency is widely reported as unpredictable, and reviewers on G2 call the dashboard overwhelming and ask for a basic mode

Compliance and scale get expensive fast: HIPAA is a $2,000/mo add-on, Zero Data Retention $1,000/mo, extra concurrency $10/line, Build retains recordings for only 14 days, and Scale pricing is quote-only with no public numbers to budget against

faq.question: How much does Vapi actually cost per minute in 2026?
faq.answer: The published rate is $0.05 per minute, but that only covers Vapi's orchestration layer. On top you pay at cost for speech-to-text (about $0.005-0.008/min), the LLM (token-based and the biggest swing factor), text-to-speech (about $0.05-0.36/min depending on the voice) and telephony (about $0.0085-0.014/min). Most complete setups land between $0.10 and $0.30 per minute all-in, and about $0.12-0.24/min on a mid-tier voice before you count LLM tokens. At 500 minutes a month that is roughly $75-125; at 10,000 minutes it is $1,500-2,500. Vapi bills provider costs at cost with no markup, so bringing your own API keys drops those line items to $0 on your Vapi invoice.

faq.question: Can you really make money selling Vapi voice agents?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is the main reason people learn the platform. The standard play is an AI receptionist for local businesses - dentists, plumbers, law firms, clinics - sold at $500-2,000 a month plus a setup fee, against a usage cost of roughly $75-125 for a 500-minute month. Outbound lead qualification is the second model: dial, qualify and book appointments, then bill per booked lead instead of per minute. A third route is white-labeling a vertical-specific agent and charging a flat monthly fee. The catch is that you are running a service business, not a SaaS - you need code skills, you own the latency problems, and one bad call experience can lose a client.

faq.question: Is Vapi free to try, and do I need to know how to code?
faq.answer: New accounts get free starter credit - widely reported around $10, plus 60+ included usage minutes - with no credit card required, which is enough to build an agent and run real test calls. It is not enough to handle customer volume, and there is no ongoing free monthly allowance. On the coding question: Vapi is aimed at developers. You can assemble a basic agent in the dashboard, but anything beyond that - custom tools, transfers, dynamic variables, latency tuning - assumes you are comfortable with APIs and webhooks. If you want a no-code product you can resell tomorrow, a bundled platform like Synthflow or Retell will be less painful, even at a higher headline rate.

features: Voice-agent orchestration that stitches your choice of STT, LLM, TTS and telephony into one bot that answers and places calls with interruption handling
Sub-second turn-taking on a tuned stack, with automatic barge-in, silence detection and call transfer to a human
REST API, SDKs and webhooks for dynamic variables, custom tools and CRM hand-off - no visual-only builder lock-in
10 concurrent calls included on the Build plan, with extra lines at $10/month for outbound campaigns
Built-in call logs and transcripts plus provider pass-through billing at cost, so you can swap models and voices without renegotiating a contract
content:
# Vapi Review 2026: The Cheapest Way to Sell AI Phone Agents

I have run Vapi agents for two clients since early 2026 - a dental office that wanted after-hours booking and a property manager who needed outbound lead qualification. The platform fee is real and it is low. The invoice that lands at the end of the month is not the number on the pricing page, and that gap is the first thing anyone building a voice-agent business has to understand.

## What Vapi Actually Is

Vapi is not a phone system and not a chatbot. It is the orchestration layer that sits between four vendors you pick yourself: a speech-to-text engine (Deepgram, AssemblyAI), an LLM (GPT, Claude, Gemini), a text-to-speech voice (ElevenLabs, Cartesia) and a telephony provider (Twilio, Vonage). You describe the agent - system prompt, tools, voice, transfer rules - and Vapi handles turn-taking, interruption handling, latency and routing. A well-tuned agent answers in under a second. There is an API, SDKs, and a dashboard for logs and transcripts.

That architecture is the point. Nothing is locked in. You can swap a $0.30/min voice for a $0.05/min one, or move from a frontier model to a small one, and watch the per-minute cost move the same day. It is also the source of the pain: four moving parts means four invoices and four places for latency to creep in.

## The Money Angle

Small businesses hate missed calls, and the numbers are brutal. A missed call at a dental office is a $300-800 patient, at a law firm a $1,000+ consult, at an HVAC company a $500 job. That pain is why people are selling AI receptionists as a service.

1. **AI receptionist for local businesses.** Build one agent template, clone it per client, charge $500-2,000 a month plus setup. Usage for a 500-minute month runs roughly $75-125. Ten clients at $800/month is $8,000 in revenue against maybe $1,000 in platform and provider costs. The margin is the business.

2. **Outbound lead qualification.** Real-estate teams, solar installers and B2B agencies pay per qualified appointment. Vapi dials, qualifies and books into a calendar, and you bill per booked lead instead of per minute - which decouples your income from call length.

3. **White-label reselling.** Rebrand the agent as your own product for a vertical - clinics, salons, trades - and charge a flat monthly fee. The client never sees Vapi.

4. **After-hours and overflow coverage.** Even businesses with a receptionist want a bot for nights and weekends. It is the easiest first sale because it replaces nobody, so there is no internal resistance to overcome.

## What It Really Costs

The published fee is $0.05 per minute, billed to the second, and that is only Vapi's orchestration cut. Everything else is passed through at cost: STT about $0.005-0.008/min, TTS about $0.05-0.36/min depending on voice, telephony about $0.0085-0.014/min plus about $2/month per number, and the LLM billed per token - which Vapi's own docs call the largest cost you control, driven by how long your system prompt is and roughly five model calls per conversation turn.

Real all-in spend lands around $0.10-0.30 per minute, and roughly $0.12-0.24/min on a mid-tier voice before tokens. That means 500 minutes is about $75-125 a month, 2,000 minutes about $300-500, and 10,000 minutes about $1,500-2,500. Bring your own API keys and Vapi charges $0 for those line items - you just pay each vendor directly, which is cheaper but more admin.

The extras are where budgets break. HIPAA compliance is a $2,000/month add-on and Zero Data Retention is $1,000/month, on top of usage. Extra concurrent lines beyond the included 10 cost $10 each per month. SMS follow-ups are $0.005 per message. Build keeps call recordings for only 14 days, which is a problem the first time you want to review a month of calls. Scale is an annual contract with quote-only pricing, so you cannot budget it in a spreadsheet.

## Where It Falls Apart

Latency. Users consistently flag it as unpredictable, and on a voice call that is not a cosmetic issue - a 1.5-second pause makes a bot feel broken. You fix it by tuning the stack, not by clicking a setting.

The dashboard is dense. Reviewers on G2 (a 4.2, off only a handful of reviews) describe it as overwhelming and ask for a simple mode. This is a tool for someone who reads logs and understands token costs, not for a solo operator who wants to hand a client a login.

And there is no compliance floor. Build ships without SSO, RBAC or SOC 2, so most mid-size companies will fail it in a security review. That pushes you to Scale, where the price is whatever the sales call says it is.

## Who Should Pay

Buy Vapi if you have engineering time, want to sell voice agents as a service, and care about the per-minute math - it is the cheapest orchestration layer you can build a business on, and the free trial credit lets you prove it before you commit.

Skip it if you want a turnkey no-code product, if you need HIPAA or SOC 2 from day one without a $2,000/month add-on, or if nobody on your team enjoys watching latency dashboards. For those cases, a bundled platform like Bland at a flat $0.14/min or Synthflow at about $0.08-0.09/min will cost more per minute and save you far more in headaches.
